title: Resolve a Customer Account Review
prerequisites: 1–6: records, goods sales, settlement, and ledger entries
question: What can we tell the customer about delivery, billing, and the amount still unsettled?
scenario: The sales coordinator is preparing a response to a design-trade customer. The warehouse has delivery information, treasury can see money received, and the controller wants the response to explain which invoices that money settles. You have been asked to assemble one account review that all three teams can use. Begin by predicting whether an undelivered order, an unpaid invoice, and unapplied cash would require the same follow-up.
scope: Customer 120, Hubbard Inc: the six orders placed from January 1 through March 31, 2024. Compare March 31 and April 30. This selection excludes other orders and is not the customer’s complete account history.
deliverable: A document timeline, two-date invoice settlement schedule, and a customer response with an action owner.

sections.title: Session 1 — Establish what was delivered and billed
sections.intro: Save a separate Case01.xlsx or Case01.sql. Keep a Review sheet or text note for the scope, decisions, and evidence. The order date selects the cohort, while shipment and invoice dates determine what had happened by the review date.
figure: handoffs
Who must contribute to the customer response?
Sales coordinator defines the six-order scope.
Operations explains shipments and remaining quantities.
Controller and treasury explain invoices, cash, and allocation.

stages.title: Define the order population
stages.question: Predict the number of rows when six orders have several lines.
stages.excel: Import `T9_SalesOrder` → `SalesOrderData`, `T10_SalesOrderLine` → `SalesOrderLineData`. In Power Query keep both imported queries unchanged. Reference SalesOrderData as SelectedOrders; filter SelectedOrders to CustomerID 120 and OrderDate on or after January 1 and before April 1, 2024. Retain the six selected rows, including SalesOrderID and OrderDate. Reference SalesOrderLineData and merge with SelectedOrders on SalesOrderID using an Inner join; expand OrderDate only. Name the result OrderLines and load it. Insert a PivotTable: Rows = SalesOrderID and OrderDate; Values = Count of SalesOrderLineID and Sum of LineTotal. Set Count explicitly; the default sum of an identifier is meaningless.
stages.check: Six orders, 22 lines. Order 29 has five lines totaling 20,969.46. The other orders are 75, 236, 185, 434, and 388.
stages.meaning: An order header identifies the customer and date, while its lines describe the separate goods. Keep the order total out of a line-level sum.
stages.keep: Save OrderLines and the six-row order summary.
stages.mismatch: If the count is larger, check the customer and order-date filter before changing any join.
stages.sqlText:
GROUP BY produces one result per order and date. COUNT counts line identifiers; SUM totals their amounts. The inner SELECT defines the fixed order population. ORDER BY makes the result repeatable.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.

stages.title: Compare ordered, shipped, and billed quantities
stages.question: Which difference would require operations to act, and which would require billing to act?
stages.excel:
Import Shipment as ShipmentData, ShipmentLine as ShipmentLineData, SalesInvoice as SalesInvoiceData, and SalesInvoiceLine as SalesInvoiceLineData before merging. Keep these raw queries unchanged. Reference ShipmentLineData as ShippedByOrderLine and merge to ShipmentData on ShipmentID; expand ShipmentDate. Filter ShipmentDate through March 31, 2024. Group by SalesOrderLineID, Sum QuantityShipped into a column named Shipped. Separately reference SalesInvoiceLineData as BilledByOrderLine; merge to SalesInvoiceData on SalesInvoiceID, expand InvoiceDate, filter through March 31, 2024, then group by SalesOrderLineID, Sum Quantity into a column named Billed. Reference OrderLines as Fulfillment and merge ShippedByOrderLine and BilledByOrderLine to it using Left outer joins on SalesOrderLineID. Expand the two totals and replace unmatched numeric nulls with 0 after checking that they mean no event. Load as Fulfillment. Add OrderedLessShipped to Fulfillment and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Fulfillment[OrderedLessShipped]"
=ROUND([@Quantity]-[@Shipped],2)
~~~

Add ShippedLessBilled and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Fulfillment[ShippedLessBilled]"
=ROUND([@Shipped]-[@Billed],2)
~~~
stages.check: 22 rows remain. Lines 924, 1515, and 1694 have ordered quantities exceeding shipments by 0.63, 3.67, and 1.63 respectively. Every line’s shipped quantity equals its billed quantity at this cutoff.
stages.meaning: The selected evidence points to incomplete fulfillment on three lines. It does not establish missing billing for goods already shipped. Those are different conclusions.
stages.keep: Save Fulfillment and identify the three lines for an operations follow-up.
stages.mismatch: More than 22 rows means a detail table was joined before summarizing. A tiny floating-point difference is not an unbilled quantity.
stages.sqlText:
WITH names two temporary results inside this statement: shipped and billed. Each is first summed by SalesOrderLineID. The final LEFT JOIN retains every selected order line, and COALESCE shows zero when no dated event exists. This avoids multiplying shipment and invoice detail against each other.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelInputs: ShipmentData ← Shipment and ShipmentLineData ← ShipmentLine (import here)
SalesInvoiceData ← SalesInvoice and SalesInvoiceLineData ← SalesInvoiceLine (import here)
excelOutputs: ShippedByOrderLine and BilledByOrderLine: one row per order line with a dated event

stages.title: Keep invoices at their own grain
stages.question: Will the number of invoices equal the number of orders?
stages.excel:
Reference the raw SalesInvoiceData imported in Session 1.2 as Invoices and Inner merge to SelectedOrders on SalesOrderID. Preserve SalesInvoiceData for other references. Keep SalesInvoiceID, SalesOrderID, InvoiceDate, and GrandTotal. Sort by InvoiceDate and SalesInvoiceID; load as Invoices. Keep all related invoice dates for now so the second session can reconstruct both cutoffs. On Review, label B4 Visible invoices and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B4"
=SUBTOTAL(103,Invoices[SalesInvoiceID])
~~~

Label B5 Visible invoice amount and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B5"
=SUBTOTAL(109,Invoices[GrandTotal])
~~~
stages.check: 20 related invoices in recorded history; 17 are dated through March 31. Do not add freight and tax again: GrandTotal already includes them.
stages.meaning: An order can be invoiced in parts. The April invoices belong in the later review, even though the orders were placed in the first quarter.
stages.keep: Save Invoices and pause. Write one sentence distinguishing cohort selection from event cutoff.
stages.mismatch: Ordinary SUM includes hidden rows. Use SUBTOTAL for filtered totals or a date-conditioned SUMIFS.
stages.sqlText:
This result has one invoice header per row. The order subquery selects the cohort, but invoice dates remain unrestricted so both reporting cutoffs can be reconstructed later.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelOutputs: Invoices: 20 selected invoice headers, including later dates

sections.stop: You should have six orders, 22 line comparisons, and 20 invoice headers. Keep the three incomplete-fulfillment lines separate from the receivables question.

sections.title: Session 2 — Reconstruct settlement and prepare the response
sections.intro: Receiving money and applying it to an invoice are separate events. Start from the invoice population, then summarize applications and credits independently.
figure: relationships
Why must settlement records be summarized separately?
One order can have several shipments and invoices.
One receipt can support several invoice applications.
Aggregate applications and credits by invoice before comparing balances.

stages.title: Read cash and credit evidence
stages.question: Predict whether adding receipt amounts down the application table would overstate this population’s settlement.
stages.excel:
Import CashReceiptApplication as CashReceiptApplicationData and CashReceipt as CashReceiptData. Reference CashReceiptApplicationData and Inner merge with Invoices on SalesInvoiceID; load as Applications. Reference CashReceiptData and load as Receipts. In Applications add ReceiptDate:

~~~text title="Excel — Applications[ReceiptDate]"
=XLOOKUP([@CashReceiptID],Receipts[CashReceiptID],Receipts[ReceiptDate],"No match",0)
~~~

Format ReceiptDate as a date and investigate any No match result. Add ReceiptAmount:

~~~text title="Excel — Applications[ReceiptAmount]"
=XLOOKUP([@CashReceiptID],Receipts[CashReceiptID],Receipts[Amount],"No match",0)
~~~

 Do not total that repeated receipt amount. Import CreditMemo as CreditMemoData. Create two references, CreditsByOrder filtered to the six SalesOrderIDs and CreditsByInvoice filtered to the 20 OriginalSalesInvoiceIDs; Append as new, then remove duplicates by CreditMemoID in Power Query. Load as Credits. Inspect OriginalSalesInvoiceID before allocating a credit.
stages.check: 24 applications across recorded history. Credit memo 30 is dated April 26 and credits invoice 1086 by 612.38. Receipt 165 appears on several application rows; its 18,938.14 must be counted only once when describing the receipt.
stages.meaning: This credit changes the April explanation. It is subsequent evidence, not a reduction that was already recorded on March 31.
stages.keep: Save Applications, Credits, and the dates of the receipt/application handoffs.
stages.mismatch: A credit found by order only needs further allocation evidence. Do not force it onto the first invoice. This worked credit has an explicit invoice link.
stages.sqlText:
Each result is one application. ReceiptAmount repeats when one receipt funds several applications. Sum AppliedAmount for invoice settlement and retain distinct receipt IDs when describing received cash.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelInputs: CashReceiptApplicationData ← CashReceiptApplication and CashReceiptData ← CashReceipt (import here)

stages.title: Build the two-date settlement schedule
stages.question: Will the later balance fall only because of cash, or can new invoices and credits change it too?
stages.excel:
Set the table names to Invoices, Applications, and Credits exactly. On Review label B2 Reporting date and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B2 — first cutoff"
=DATE(2024,3,31)
~~~

In Invoices add Applied:

~~~text title="Excel — Invoices[Applied]"
=SUMIFS(Applications[AppliedAmount],Applications[SalesInvoiceID],[@SalesInvoiceID],Applications[ApplicationDate],"<="&Review!$B$2)
~~~

Add Credited:

~~~text title="Excel — Invoices[Credited]"
=SUMIFS(Credits[GrandTotal],Credits[OriginalSalesInvoiceID],[@SalesInvoiceID],Credits[CreditMemoDate],"<="&Review!$B$2)
~~~

Add Remaining:

~~~text title="Excel — Invoices[Remaining]"
=ROUND([@GrandTotal]-[@Applied]-[@Credited],2)
~~~

Filter InvoiceDate through the date in Review!B2. Label Review!B6 Visible remaining balance and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B6"
=SUBTOTAL(109,Invoices[Remaining])
~~~

Save a values-only snapshot of the visible rows with its cutoff label. Replace Review!B2 with the second date, update the InvoiceDate filter, and repeat:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B2 — second cutoff"
=DATE(2024,4,30)
~~~

Keep the formulas in the working table for refresh. Copy only visible cells when retaining a filtered snapshot; alternatively filter the query before loading each dated view.
stages.check: March 31: 17 invoices, 72,676.21 billed, 44,067.35 applied, zero credits, and 28,608.86 remaining. April 30: 20 invoices, 75,742.57 billed, 67,836.87 applied, 612.38 credited, and 7,293.32 remaining.
stages.meaning: The balance fell by 21,315.54 while new invoices added 3,066.36. A statement that “cash collected equals the fall in receivables” would miss both new billing and the credit.
stages.keep: Save the two schedules and a change bridge: new invoices less additional applications less new credits.
stages.mismatch: Check application dates, not just receipt dates. A final Paid status cannot reconstruct an earlier balance.
stages.sqlText:
The cutoffs result contains the two review dates. CROSS JOIN pairs each date with each selected invoice, and the invoice-date condition excludes bills not yet issued. Each correlated SUM reads only applications or credits for that invoice through that date. Summarize the resulting rows separately by AsOf.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelOutputs: Invoices: cutoff-dependent Applied, Credited, and Remaining columns

stages.title: Check accounting and assign the response
stages.question: Which event reduces receivables: cash receipt or cash application?
stages.excel: Import GLEntry as GLEntryData and Account as AccountData. Keep GLEntryData in Power Query and filter references before loading: SourceDocumentType/SourceDocumentID pairs SalesInvoice/68, CashReceipt/43, CashReceiptApplication/47, CreditMemo/30. Use four filtered references and Append as new; do not filter all four IDs without their document types. Merge AccountData on AccountID. Load the 10 rows as SelectedLedger. Insert a PivotTable with VoucherNumber in Rows and sums of Debit and Credit in Values. Check each complete voucher balances.
stages.check: 10 posting rows in four balanced vouchers. Receipt 43 debits cash and credits customer deposits by 1,413.08. Application 47 moves that amount from deposits to receivables two days later.
stages.meaning: A supported response distinguishes operations follow-up from accounting follow-up. Explain the 7,293.32 selected balance at April 30, acknowledge credit 30, and ask operations to confirm the three earlier fulfillment gaps against later shipments before promising delivery.
stages.keep: Retain the voucher check and write a 200–300 word customer response with one named role responsible for each next action.
stages.mismatch: Filtering to the AR account alone makes a voucher appear unbalanced. Restore all lines of each selected event.
stages.sqlText:
Keep each SourceDocumentType/SourceDocumentID pair together. The same numeric ID can occur in unrelated source tables. Joining Account adds names without changing the posting grain.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelInputs: GLEntryData ← GLEntry and AccountData ← Account (import here)

sections.stop: Save the two cutoff schedules, the event-to-accounting check, and your response. Another reader should be able to reproduce every amount from the six-order scope.

finalFigure: timeline
What changed between the two reviews?
March 31: selected invoices less applications leave 28,608.86.
April adds invoices, applications, and credit memo 30.
April 30: the same order cohort leaves 7,293.32.
interpretation: The worked result supports a focused customer-account response, not an assertion about every balance Hubbard Inc has ever held. Operations addresses quantities, customer accounting confirms allocations and credits, and treasury supplies receipt evidence. A plausible next action is to confirm the later fulfillment position and contact the customer about the remaining selected invoices with the two-date schedule attached.
challenge: Select customer 120’s orders dated April 1–June 30, 2024. Reconstruct June 30 and July 31. Retain the cohort, invoice schedule, applications, credits, and one complete voucher. Explain whether the same action priorities still make sense.
hint: Change the order-cohort dates separately from the event cutoffs. Rebuild the invoice list rather than reusing the worked case’s 20 IDs. A valid result can have no credits or no remaining balance.
criteria: Assess correct population, separate event dates, no repeated receipt totals, complete voucher checks, and an action justified by the observed evidence.
readiness: Complete your chosen Excel or SQL setup. Preserve source row keys and check row counts, unique keys, and amounts after descriptive joins.
Before starting, state the cohort, cutoff, row key, independently aggregated measures, and one evidence limitation.
Keep the order cohort fixed while changing event cutoffs. Distinguish receipt from application and balance each complete voucher.

title: Review Design Work and Billing
question: How does design effort become approved work, billed amounts, and recorded cost?
scenario: The design lead is preparing a quarterly review with the controller. Several engagements overlap, and a busy month does not necessarily mean that the same month contains all related invoices. You will explain the relationship before suggesting where the lead should spend follow-up time. Predict which date describes work and which date establishes billing.
scope: Service work dated January 1–March 31, 2024: 204 time entries across 21 engagements. Begin with engagement 2, then use the whole defined population. Select billing periods by their work coverage and retain the invoice dates separately.
deliverable: An engagement-period reconciliation, an hours/billing/cost bridge, and a design review memo.

sections.title: Session 1 — Establish the work and its terms
sections.intro: Create Case02.xlsx or Case02.sql. Your Review note should distinguish work performed, approved billable hours, invoiced amounts, and cost evidence. Each has a different purpose.
figure: responsibilities
Who turns time into a customer bill?
Design lead establishes engagement terms and staffing.
Staff record billable and non-billable time; approval supports billing.
Billing connects covered time to an invoice; the controller compares measures.

stages.title: Read engagement terms
stages.question: Does a planned-hours figure establish how much work actually occurred?
stages.excel:
Import ServiceTimeEntry as ServiceTimeEntryData; reference it as TimeData and filter WorkDate from January 1 through March 31, 2024. Load as TimeData. Import ServiceEngagement as Engagements. Filter TimeData to ServiceEngagementID 2 and inspect its dates before clearing the filter. Add a column named HourlyRate to TimeData and paste this formula into its first data row; copy it down through the table column if Excel does not fill it automatically:

~~~text title="Excel — TimeData[HourlyRate]"
=XLOOKUP([@ServiceEngagementID],Engagements[ServiceEngagementID],Engagements[HourlyRate],"No match",0)
~~~

The final 0 requires an exact match. Investigate No match rather than treating it as a zero rate. In Power Query create a Reference of the filtered time query as SelectedEngagements, keep ServiceEngagementID, remove duplicates, and merge with Engagements; load as SelectedEngagements. The reference reads the imported query, so worksheet formula columns are not required for this selection.
stages.check: 21 engagement terms. Engagement 2 belongs to customer 30, has 69.59 planned hours, and an hourly rate of 210. Its start and end dates are January 12 and February 29.
stages.meaning: The terms provide a rate and planning context. They do not replace recorded hours or establish whether time was approved.
stages.keep: Save the selected engagement list and engagement 2’s terms.
stages.mismatch: A lookup is appropriate here because ServiceEngagementID is unique in the terms table. Confirm 21 distinct keys before merging.
stages.sqlText: Run each statement separately in the SQL editor. Save its text and result with the stage title. Read the result at the grain described in the question and compare the checkpoint before continuing.
excelInputs: ServiceTimeEntryData ← ServiceTimeEntry (import here; filter Q1 2024 into TimeData)
excelOutputs: TimeData: 204 time-entry rows with HourlyRate formula

stages.title: Separate time, approval, and cost
stages.question: Will all first-quarter work be approved by the quarter end?
stages.excel:
In TimeData add WorkMonth:

~~~text title="Excel — TimeData[WorkMonth]"
=DATE(YEAR([@WorkDate]),MONTH([@WorkDate]),1)
~~~

Format WorkMonth as yyyy-mm. Add ApprovedBillable; the numeric-date check prevents a blank approval from counting as approved:

~~~text title="Excel — TimeData[ApprovedBillable]"
=IF(AND(ISNUMBER([@ApprovedDate]),[@ApprovedDate]<=DATE(2024,3,31)),[@BillableHours],0)
~~~

Insert a PivotTable with ServiceEngagementID and WorkMonth in Rows; Values = Count of ServiceTimeEntryID and sums of BillableHours, NonBillableHours, ApprovedBillable, ExtendedCost. Rename the last measure RecordedTimeCost. Clear worksheet filters before creating the PivotTable; its source should include all 204 imported rows.
stages.check: 33 engagement-month groups. Total billable hours 1,409.88; non-billable hours 73.62; recorded time cost 49,022.40. No selected entry remains unapproved at March 31. Engagement 2 has 32.67 billable hours in January and 36.92 in February.
stages.meaning: An empty exception list is a finding about this criterion and scope. It does not justify inventing an approval problem. Non-billable time still consumes staff capacity and contributes to the recorded cost measure.
stages.keep: Save the 33-row summary and the approval cutoff check.
stages.mismatch: Use actual date types. A text date or an empty date treated as zero can distort the approval test.
stages.sqlText:
substr(WorkDate,1,7) creates a month key from the stored ISO date. GROUP BY engagement and month keeps different engagements separate. CASE includes billable hours only when approval occurred by the cutoff.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.

sections.stop: Save terms, the 204-row source selection, and the engagement-month summary. Write what each total includes before adding invoice data.

sections.title: Session 2 — Connect covered time to billing
sections.intro: A time row is not a billing row. Aggregate within the billing period before comparing hours to avoid repeating each invoice amount for every time entry.
figure: billing
How does a billing period connect time and invoice evidence?
Time is identified by engagement and work date.
A billing line supplies an inclusive start/end period and billed hours.
SalesInvoiceLine identifies the invoice; InvoiceDate establishes billing timing.

stages.title: Build the period reconciliation
stages.question: What happens if you join all engagement time directly to every billing line?
stages.excel:
Import ServiceBillingLine as ServiceBillingLineData; reference it as Billing and filter BillingPeriodStartDate on or after January 1, 2024 and BillingPeriodEndDate before April 1, 2024. Load as Billing. Import SalesInvoiceLine as InvoiceLines and SalesInvoice as Invoices. Keep ServiceBillingLineID as the unique row key. In Billing add SalesInvoiceID using the unique invoice-line key:

~~~text title="Excel — Billing[SalesInvoiceID]"
=XLOOKUP([@SalesInvoiceLineID],InvoiceLines[SalesInvoiceLineID],InvoiceLines[SalesInvoiceID],"No match",0)
~~~

Add InvoiceDate using the unique invoice header key, then format it as a date:

~~~text title="Excel — Billing[InvoiceDate]"
=XLOOKUP([@SalesInvoiceID],Invoices[SalesInvoiceID],Invoices[InvoiceDate],"No match",0)
~~~

Resolve any No match before calculating the approval comparison. Add CoveredBillable:

~~~text title="Excel — Billing[CoveredBillable]"
=SUMIFS(TimeData[BillableHours],TimeData[ServiceEngagementID],[@ServiceEngagementID],TimeData[WorkDate],">="&[@BillingPeriodStartDate],TimeData[WorkDate],"<="&[@BillingPeriodEndDate])
~~~

Add HoursApprovedByInvoice; approval must be present and no later than the invoice date:

~~~text title="Excel — Billing[HoursApprovedByInvoice]"
=SUMIFS(TimeData[BillableHours],TimeData[ServiceEngagementID],[@ServiceEngagementID],TimeData[WorkDate],">="&[@BillingPeriodStartDate],TimeData[WorkDate],"<="&[@BillingPeriodEndDate],TimeData[ApprovedDate],">0",TimeData[ApprovedDate],"<="&[@InvoiceDate])
~~~

Add HoursDifference:

~~~text title="Excel — Billing[HoursDifference]"
=ROUND([@BilledHours]-[@HoursApprovedByInvoice],2)
~~~
stages.check: 33 billing lines cover 1,409.88 hours and 244,865.45 of line amounts. Every billed-hours comparison agrees. Billing line 2 covers January 12–30 for engagement 2; its 32.67 hours become 6,860.70 on invoice 241 dated January 31.
stages.meaning: Coverage dates explain which work is billed. Invoice date explains when it is invoiced. A future population may have uncovered time, overlapping periods, or approval after invoicing. Retain those exceptions rather than filling in a match. For a complete accounting checkpoint, retrieve invoice 241 and explain why approved time creates no additional revenue posting. Follow the paired Excel and SQL procedure in [Lesson 7](../../learn-and-practice/follow-design-time-into-billing.md#3-retrieve-the-invoice-voucher). Keep this single-engagement example separate from the case population.
stages.keep: Save Billing and a zero/nonzero HoursDifference check.
stages.mismatch: If totals multiply, check whether you merged raw time rows into Billing. SUMIFS keeps the billing row unique. Compare period boundaries inclusively.
stages.sqlText:
The correlated SUM uses the billing line’s engagement and inclusive coverage dates, plus approval by InvoiceDate. It returns one hours total per billing row without expanding that row once for every time entry.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelInputs: ServiceBillingLineData ← ServiceBillingLine (import here; filter Q1 2024 into Billing)
InvoiceLines ← SalesInvoiceLine and Invoices ← SalesInvoice (import here)
excelOutputs: Billing: billing-line detail with invoice date, covered hours, and approval comparison

stages.title: Compare effort, price, and limited cost
stages.question: Does the difference between billed amounts and recorded time cost equal engagement profit?
stages.excel:
Create a PivotTable from TimeData with ServiceEngagementID and WorkMonth in Rows and sums of BillableHours, NonBillableHours, and ExtendedCost in Values. In Billing add WorkMonth:

~~~text title="Excel — Billing[WorkMonth]"
=DATE(YEAR([@BillingPeriodStartDate]),MONTH([@BillingPeriodStartDate]),1)
~~~

Format WorkMonth as yyyy-mm. Create a second PivotTable from Billing using the same Rows and sums of BilledHours and LineAmount. Align the summaries by engagement and month, not row position. For engagement 2 inspect January and February separately. On Review label B2 Quarter billable share, enter the formula below, and format it as a percentage:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B2"
=SUM(TimeData[BillableHours])/(SUM(TimeData[BillableHours])+SUM(TimeData[NonBillableHours]))
~~~

Label B3 Billed amounts less recorded time cost and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B3"
=SUM(Billing[LineAmount])-SUM(TimeData[ExtendedCost])
~~~

These totals use the full Q1 imported populations; ordinary SUM includes rows hidden by worksheet filters. Create a clustered-column chart from engagement-level billable and non-billable hours using the verified summary.
stages.check: Engagement 2: January billed amount 6,860.70 and time cost 937.02; February 7,753.20 and 1,042.22. Quarter billable share is 95.04%; billed amounts less recorded time cost is 195,843.05.
stages.meaning: The release supports an hours-to-billing reconciliation and a limited time-cost comparison. It does not allocate every overhead, selling, support, or financing cost to each engagement. Also, an invoice does not establish cash collection. Use Case 1 to investigate settlement.
stages.keep: Retain the matched summaries, chart, and a 250-word memo explaining one follow-up and one limitation.
stages.mismatch: Do not subtract a full employee’s payroll from each engagement. Work-date cost and invoice-date revenue need aligned coverage before comparison.
stages.sqlText:
effort and billing each return one aggregate row before they are combined. The ratio uses all selected hours, while the difference compares billed line amounts with recorded time cost within the stated boundary.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelOutputs: Review: billable share and limited cost comparison; chart

sections.stop: Your memo should explain that the worked hours reconcile, state the cost boundary, and recommend a targeted review of non-billable effort or engagement terms without alleging missing billing.

finalFigure: bridge
Which measures belong in the design review?
1,409.88 billable hours and 73.62 non-billable hours describe effort.
33 billing lines total 244,865.45 for covered work.
Time cost of 49,022.40 supports a limited comparison, not complete profit.
interpretation: The reconciliation does not reveal unapproved quarter-end time or a billed-hours mismatch in this population. A useful management response is to discuss where non-billable effort occurred and whether it was planned, while preserving the distinction between billing rates and staff-cost snapshots. The evidence supports a focused operational conversation, not a claim that all engagements are equally profitable.
challenge: Repeat the investigation for April–June 2024 work. Rebuild the engagement and billing-period populations. Identify one changed result, inspect its source rows, and explain whether it reflects mix, timing, price, non-billable effort, or unresolved evidence.
hint: Begin with the new work-date population. Check whether each billing period stays inside the selected quarter before comparing its entire amount with quarter-only time.
criteria: Assess population completeness, approval-date handling, unique billing rows, aligned coverage, precise cost labels, and a conclusion supported by source evidence.
readiness: Complete your chosen Excel or SQL setup. Preserve source row keys and check row counts, unique keys, and amounts after descriptive joins.
Before starting, state the cohort, cutoff, row key, independently aggregated measures, and one evidence limitation.
Distinguish work dates, approval dates, billing coverage, and invoice dates when summarizing hours and costs at engagement/month grain.

title: Explain Supplier Obligations at Month End
question: Which selected obligations are uninvoiced receipts, supplier payables, or remaining estimates?
scenario: Accounts payable and the controller are reviewing quarter-end obligations. Receiving knows what arrived, AP knows which bills were received, and the controller has expense estimates awaiting later evidence. You will prepare two schedules and explain how each changes through June. Predict whether a later payment changes the liability that existed on March 31.
scope: Supplier 27’s five first-quarter 2024 goods receipts, plus the separate repairs-and-maintenance accrual journals 9, 26, and 43. Review March 31 and subsequent evidence through June 30. The accruals are a separate population, not purchases from supplier 27.
deliverable: Separate goods and expense-obligation schedules, selected posting checks, and a quarter-end review note.

sections.title: Session 1 — Follow received goods into supplier liabilities
sections.intro: Create Case03.xlsx or Case03.sql. Label the goods schedule and accrual schedule separately. A purchase order records a commitment, while a receipt establishes arrival.
figure: branches
Why do purchasing obligations follow two paths?
Goods: order, receipt, supplier invoice, payment.
Services: estimate, linked invoice, residual adjustment, payment.
Keep the two selected populations separate before interpreting obligations.

stages.title: Select the receipt population
stages.question: How many receipt lines might one supplier order produce?
stages.excel: Import PurchaseOrder as PurchaseOrderData, GoodsReceipt as GoodsReceiptData, and GoodsReceiptLine as GoodsReceiptLineData. Preserve all three raw queries. Reference PurchaseOrderData as SupplierOrders and filter SupplierID 27. Reference GoodsReceiptData as SelectedGoodsReceipts and filter ReceiptDate January 1 through March 31, 2024; Inner merge to SupplierOrders on PurchaseOrderID. Reference GoodsReceiptLineData, merge to SelectedGoodsReceipts on GoodsReceiptID, and expand ReceiptDate. Load as Receipts. Preserve GoodsReceiptLineID, POLineID, QuantityReceived, and ExtendedStandardCost.
stages.check: Five receipts and five lines; standard receipt cost totals 7,234.30. Receipt IDs are 174, 175, 253, 396, and 340.
stages.meaning: The receipt amount is inventory at standard cost. The supplier invoice may contain a different purchase cost or tax, so receipt cost cannot simply be subtracted from invoice GrandTotal to calculate GRNI.

title: Choose a Product and Pricing Priority
question: Which product group deserves a focused review, and what evidence supports that priority?
scenario: Commercial leadership has time for one product review. The sales coordinator proposes reviewing discounts, while the controller asks whether product mix, cost assumptions, or delivery performance could explain the same pattern. Your job is to compare those explanations and recommend a bounded next investigation, not to declare a product group unprofitable from one percentage.
scope: Goods invoice lines dated January 1–March 31, 2024. Compare product groups using the same population. Credits are a separate credit-date population. Current product-master attributes and standard costs are descriptive reference data, not historical snapshots.
deliverable: A product comparison, selected pricing evidence, a simple analytical chart, and a recommendation memo.

~~~text title="Excel — ProductReview[Realization]"
=IF([@ListValue]=0,NA(),[@LineTotal]/[@ListValue])
~~~

Add StandardMargin:

~~~text title="Excel — ProductReview[StandardMargin]"
=[@LineTotal]-[@CurrentStandardCost]
~~~

Add StandardMarginPct:

~~~text title="Excel — ProductReview[StandardMarginPct]"
=IF([@LineTotal]=0,NA(),[@StandardMargin]/[@LineTotal])
~~~

title: Explain Production Cost and Delivery Pressure
question: Do completion, recorded cost, and financial close tell the same production story?

The controller asks whether late completion, material usage, labor support, and cost variance point to the same cause. You will examine the January release cohort, trace two work orders, and identify the operational evidence needed before recommending a change.
scope: 336 work orders released January 1–31, 2024, with events assessed through February 29. Begin with work order 1 and compare work order 67. Capacity comparisons cover all scheduled work in the selected work centers and dates, not only the January cohort.
deliverable: A work-order cost bridge, completion/close comparison, capacity evidence, and a production review memo.

sections.title: Session 1 — Define the cohort and read the plan
sections.intro: Create Case05.xlsx or Case05.sql. A release-date cohort stays fixed even when completion or close occurs in a later month. Keep actual event dates visible.
figure: planning
How does a plan become production evidence?
A recommendation and work order describe intended supply.
Operations and daily schedules describe planned work-center activity.
Actual events establish issue, completion, and financial close.

stages.title: Keep the release cohort fixed
stages.question: Would filtering by completion month answer the same question as filtering by release month?
stages.excel:
Import WorkOrder as WorkOrderData. Reference it as Orders and filter ReleasedDate January 1–31, 2024, preserving the raw query. Load as Orders, keeping IDs and all date fields. Label Review!B2 Release cohort and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B2"
=ROWS(Orders[WorkOrderID])
~~~

Add CompletedByCutoff to Orders:

~~~text title="Excel — Orders[CompletedByCutoff]"
=IF(AND(ISNUMBER([@CompletedDate]),[@CompletedDate]<=DATE(2024,2,29)),1,0)
~~~

Add ClosedByCutoff:

~~~text title="Excel — Orders[ClosedByCutoff]"
=IF(AND(ISNUMBER([@ClosedDate]),[@ClosedDate]<=DATE(2024,2,29)),1,0)
~~~

Add MissingPlanLink:

~~~text title="Excel — Orders[MissingPlanLink]"
=IF([@SupplyPlanRecommendationID]="",1,0)
~~~

Do not filter away missing dates or links.
stages.check: 336 released orders; 336 completed by February 29 but only 290 closed. 136 completed after their due date. One lacks a planning link; one has completion before release.
stages.meaning: Completion and close measure different responsibilities. A chronology anomaly also means these dates require source follow-up before a scheduling recommendation relies on them.
stages.keep: Save Orders and the timing counts, including the exceptions.
stages.mismatch: Current Status is not an as-of measure. Test the actual dates against the cutoff and retain missing links.
stages.sqlText: Run each statement separately in the SQL editor. Save its text and result with the stage title. Read the result at the grain described in the question and compare the checkpoint before continuing.
excelOutputs: Orders: fixed January 2024 release cohort; 336 rows, missing dates retained

stages.title: Trace the two operation paths
stages.question: Can a work order be completed in the file even when its operation support is missing?

Reference WorkOrderOperationData as SelectedOperations and filter WorkOrderID 1 or 67. Reference WorkOrderOperationScheduleData as ScheduleByOperation, filter ScheduleDate through February 29, 2024, and group by WorkOrderOperationID, Sum ScheduledHours as ScheduledHours. Reference SelectedOperations as OperationTrace, Left merge ScheduleByOperation on WorkOrderOperationID, and sort by WorkOrderID then OperationSequence. Keep PlannedLoadHours and actual start/end dates beside the schedule total.
stages.check: Four operation rows for work order 67, progressing through work centers 1–4. No operation rows are returned for work order 1. WO67’s scheduled hours are 9.47, 19.28, 11.45, and 4.44 by operation sequence.
stages.meaning: The absence of operation detail for WO1 is an evidence limitation, not proof that no work happened. Other documents still record its material issue and completion. Compare support completeness before inferring efficiency.
stages.keep: Save the operation trace and a note about WO1’s missing support.
stages.mismatch: An Inner join from Orders to Operations would hide WO1 from the cohort summary, so retain the prescribed Left join.
stages.sqlText: Run each statement separately in the SQL editor. Save its text and result with the stage title. Read the result at the grain described in the question and compare the checkpoint before continuing.

sections.title: Session 2 — Build costs at one row per work order
sections.intro: Materials, labor support, completions, and close records each have their own grain. Summarize them separately before merging to the cohort.
figure: costs
What changes when materials become finished goods?
Material issue moves component cost into work in process.
Completion records finished goods at standard material and conversion cost.
Close records material and conversion variances after completion.

stages.title: Prepare the four event summaries
stages.question: How would joining raw issue lines to raw labor entries change the totals?
stages.excel: Import MaterialIssueLine as MaterialIssueLineData, MaterialIssue as MaterialIssueData, LaborTimeEntry as LaborTimeEntryData, ProductionCompletionLine as ProductionCompletionLineData, ProductionCompletion as ProductionCompletionData, and WorkOrderClose as WorkOrderCloseData. Keep those raw queries unchanged. Create four references and summarize before merging. IssuesByWorkOrder: merge MaterialIssueLineData to MaterialIssueData on MaterialIssueID, filter IssueDate through February 29, group by WorkOrderID and sum ExtendedStandardCost as Issued. LaborByWorkOrder: filter LaborTimeEntryData WorkDate through February 29, group by WorkOrderID and sum ExtendedLaborCost as LaborSupport. CompletionsByWorkOrder: merge ProductionCompletionLineData to ProductionCompletionData on ProductionCompletionID, filter CompletionDate through February 29, group by WorkOrderID and sum QuantityCompleted as CompletedQty, ExtendedStandardMaterialCost as CompletedMaterials, ExtendedStandardConversionCost as CompletedConversion, and ExtendedStandardTotalCost as CompletedTotal. ClosesByWorkOrder: filter WorkOrderCloseData CloseDate through February 29, group by WorkOrderID and sum MaterialVarianceAmount as MaterialVariance, ConversionVarianceAmount as ConversionVariance, and TotalVarianceAmount as TotalVariance. Reference Orders as CostBridge and Left merge these four unique-key summaries on WorkOrderID; load as CostBridge. Replace missing issue/labor/completion totals with zero only after checking event absence. Leave missing close variances blank, meaning no close by cutoff.

stages.meaning: Material issue less standard material completion equals the material variance for this closed example. Labor support is one input into actual conversion cost rather than its complete measure. Do not force it to equal completion conversion plus close variance.
stages.keep: Save CostBridge and a WO1 bridge with units and cost basis labeled.
stages.mismatch: ConversionVarianceAmount already combines direct labor and overhead variance, so adding those components again would double-count them.
stages.sqlText:
Four named results summarize issues, labor, completions, and closes separately by WorkOrderID. LEFT JOIN adds these totals to the fixed release cohort. Missing close totals stay null, distinguishing an unclosed order from a zero variance.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelInputs: MaterialIssueLineData ← MaterialIssueLine and MaterialIssueData ← MaterialIssue (import here)
ProductionCompletionLineData ← ProductionCompletionLine and ProductionCompletionData ← ProductionCompletion (import here)
excelOutputs: IssuesByWorkOrder, LaborByWorkOrder, CompletionsByWorkOrder, ClosesByWorkOrder: separate one-row-per-work-order summaries
CostBridge: all 336 cohort orders; unclosed variance remains null

stages.title: Compare a contrasting cost result
stages.question: Is the largest absolute variance also the largest variance relative to output?
stages.excel:
In CostBridge add AbsVariance; leave unclosed orders blank:

~~~text title="Excel — CostBridge[AbsVariance]"
=IF([@TotalVariance]="","",ABS([@TotalVariance]))
~~~

Filter TotalVariance nonblank and sort AbsVariance descending. Inspect WO67. Retain the ReleasedDate, DueDate, CompletedDate, and ClosedDate columns carried from Orders in the previous merges. Compare WO1 and WO67 on completed quantity, total completion cost, material variance, and conversion variance. Add VariancePerCompletedUnit only where a close exists and completed quantity is positive:

~~~text title="Excel — CostBridge[VariancePerCompletedUnit]"
=IF(OR([@TotalVariance]="",[@CompletedQty]<=0),"",[@TotalVariance]/[@CompletedQty])
~~~

Keep LaborSupport in a separate column.
stages.check: WO67 has the largest absolute closed variance in this cohort: 5,463.38, including 647.23 material and 4,816.15 conversion. It completed 32.99 units at 20,387.82 standard total cost. It completed February 7 against a February 4 due date and closed February 13.
stages.meaning: The larger absolute variance partly reflects scale. It also has operation support that WO1 lacks. Inspect the dates and cost components before attributing the difference to worker productivity or a particular work center.
stages.keep: Save the two-order comparison and two competing explanations.
stages.mismatch: A blank variance is not a zero variance. Rank closed orders only and show the 46 orders not yet closed separately.
stages.sqlText:
This repeats the same independently aggregated cost method for WO1 and WO67. It runs independently without a temporary table from an earlier step.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelOutputs: Review: separate WO1/WO67 cost and timing comparison

sections.stop: Your cost bridge should preserve 336 orders and separate missing close evidence from zero variances. Save the two-order comparison before examining capacity.

sections.title: Session 3 — Relate timing to capacity and recommend a follow-up
sections.intro: A cohort’s late completion can coincide with capacity pressure without proving causation. Compare dates and work centers, then identify the evidence needed to test the explanation.
figure: grains
Which totals can be joined without multiplication?
Summarize issue, labor, completion, and close independently by work order.
Join each one-row summary to the fixed 336-order cohort.
Analyze daily work-center capacity separately from order cost.

stages.title: Look beneath the period capacity total
stages.question: Could total scheduled hours be below capacity while individual days are over capacity?
stages.excel:
Reference the raw WorkOrderOperationScheduleData as LoadByCenterDay, filter ScheduleDate January 1–February 29, 2024, group by WorkCenterID and ScheduleDate, and sum ScheduledHours. Import WorkCenterCalendar as WorkCenterCalendarData. Reference it as DailyCapacity and filter CalendarDate to the same dates. Left merge DailyCapacity to LoadByCenterDay on WorkCenterID and CalendarDate = ScheduleDate, selecting keys in that order. Replace unmatched scheduled totals with zero after checking for schedule dates absent from the calendar: reference LoadByCenterDay as UnmatchedScheduleDates and Left anti merge to DailyCapacity on the same two keys, in the same order. In Power Query add a Custom Column named AboveCapacity:

~~~text title="Power Query — Daily capacity / AboveCapacity"
if [ScheduledHours] > [AvailableHours] then 1 else 0
~~~

 Preserve DailyCapacity; reference it as CapacityByCenter and group by WorkCenterID to sum available hours, scheduled hours, and AboveCapacity. For WO67’s centers inspect daily rows around January 30–February 5.
stages.check: Assembly: 9,230.89 available hours, 5,316.59 scheduled, but two days above capacity. Finishing and Test has seven days above capacity. Period totals alone conceal daily peaks.
stages.meaning: This capacity comparison covers all scheduled work, so it provides context for the cohort rather than allocating all capacity pressure to it. Available work-center hours are not interchangeable with employee paid hours.
stages.keep: Save the center summary and one daily detail view supporting or weakening your explanation.
stages.mismatch: Keep calendar dates with no load. Check calendar coverage before concluding there are no overloaded days.
stages.sqlText:
Daily schedule totals are joined to the calendar before work-center aggregation. DaysAboveCapacity preserves daily peaks that a comparison of period totals would hide.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelOutputs: LoadByCenterDay: one schedule total per center/day
DailyCapacity: one calendar capacity row per center/day; retained for inspection

stages.title: Prepare the production review
stages.question: What can you recommend now, and what still needs an operational explanation?
stages.excel: Build Review with three sections: cohort timing, two-order cost comparison, and capacity context. Link their verified results. Create a column chart for the five centers’ counts of days above capacity. Write a recommendation that names the planner or production role, identifies a specific date/center or missing record to inspect, and explains how that inspection would affect the proposed schedule change.
stages.check: The worked evidence shows 46 completed but unclosed orders, missing operation support for WO1, and daily capacity peaks despite spare period totals. These are distinct follow-ups.
stages.meaning: Recommend checking daily scheduling and missing support before changing staffing or treating variance as inefficiency. A cost variance, a late completion, and a documentation gap need not share one cause.
stages.keep: Save a 400–500 word memo with one prioritized action and a stated alternative explanation.
stages.mismatch: Do not claim that spare aggregate hours prove enough capacity on every day, or that standard-cost variance measures cash overspending.
stages.sqlText: Use the saved result tables from the preceding stages to construct this comparison and written interpretation. Retain the query names, filters, source keys, and amounts in your case notes. An ordered result table can communicate the comparison without making a chart or switching tools.
excelInputs: Orders, CostBridge, DailyCapacity, and CapacityByCenter (earlier stages)
excelOutputs: Review: timing, cost, and capacity sections; recommendation and chart

sections.stop: Save a reproducible cost bridge and a bounded recommendation. Keep unresolved evidence visible.

title: Explain Staffing, Overtime, and Payroll Cost
question: What do staffing plans, approved work, and paid cost actually establish?
scenario: The operations planner is considering an overtime response. Payroll asks whether the concern is planned coverage, actual hours, pay calculation, or settlement. You will compare those forms of evidence before recommending a response. Begin by predicting why a work-center workload total might differ from employees’ approved hours even when both are correct.
scope: January 1–28, 2024, using complete payroll periods 1 and 2. Begin with Assembly work center 2, then compare centers and the company-wide period payroll. Payment and remittance dates extend beyond the work window.
deliverable: A coverage comparison, employee-period pay reconciliation, settlement schedule, and staffing recommendation.

sections.title: Session 1 — Compare planned and approved hours
sections.intro: Create Case06.xlsx or Case06.sql. State the grain of each source before joining it. Raw punches, approved time, productive labor allocations, and service time serve different purposes.
figure: attendance
Which evidence describes an employee’s work?
Roster records expected attendance and location.
Punches are raw observations; approved time records authorized payroll hours.
Payroll calculates pay from its approved support and other pay rules.

stages.title: Build compatible center summaries
stages.question: Would joining every roster row to every production schedule row give a valid total?
stages.excel: Import WorkCenter as WorkCenterData, EmployeeShiftRoster as EmployeeShiftRosterData, WorkOrderOperationSchedule as WorkOrderOperationScheduleData, and TimeClockEntry as TimeClockEntryData. Keep these raw queries unchanged. Reference EmployeeShiftRosterData as RosterByCenter; filter RosterDate January 1–28, 2024 and RosterStatus Scheduled or Reassigned, then group by WorkCenterID, Sum ScheduledHours as RosteredHours. Reference WorkOrderOperationScheduleData as OperationLoadByCenter; filter ScheduleDate to the same dates, then group by WorkCenterID, Sum ScheduledHours as OperationHours. Reference TimeClockEntryData as ApprovedTime; filter WorkDate January 1–28, 2024, PayrollPeriodID 1 or 2, and ClockStatus Approved. Keep ApprovedTime at TimeClockEntryID detail, including EmployeeID, PayrollPeriodID, WorkCenterID, RegularHours, and OvertimeHours for Session 2. Reference ApprovedTime as WorkedByCenter and group by WorkCenterID, Sum RegularHours as RegularHours and Sum OvertimeHours as OvertimeHours. Reference WorkCenterData as Coverage and Left merge RosterByCenter, OperationLoadByCenter, and WorkedByCenter on WorkCenterID; load Coverage. Retain each summary’s null-center row separately for review: the master-center merge cannot display an unassigned location. Keep ApprovedTime available in Power Query; do not group or replace this detail query.
stages.check: Assembly has 2,033.11 rostered hours, 673.91 operation hours, 1,988.59 approved regular hours, and 177.92 approved overtime hours.
stages.meaning: Scheduled operation hours describe production activity, while rostered hours describe people's planned presence. Their difference is not automatically idle time. Employees may perform support work outside the operation schedule.
stages.keep: Save Coverage and a short explanation of each denominator.
stages.mismatch: Do not compute a staffing deficit by subtracting unlike hour measures without a documented labor requirement per operation.
stages.sqlText:
Roster, load, and worked are separate work-center summaries. Their units and inclusion rules remain visible even though they share a center key. The center master retains centers with no activity.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.

excelOutputs: ApprovedTime: retained approved TimeClockEntryID detail for January 1–28, 2024 / periods 1 and 2
RosterByCenter, OperationLoadByCenter, and WorkedByCenter: separate summaries

Reference it as AbsenceDetail, filter AbsenceDate January 1–28, 2024, and merge the raw EmployeeShiftRosterData on EmployeeShiftRosterID to obtain WorkCenterID. sections.title: Session 2 — Reconcile employee-period pay
sections.intro: Move from a location view to an employee-period view. One employee’s entire pay must not repeat once for each work center or time entry.

At what level should pay be connected?
Approved time can have many employee-day rows.
Summarize hours by employee and payroll period.
Join to a unique employee-period payroll register; retain location analysis separately.

stages.title: Build the pay bridge
stages.question: Will every payroll register have hourly time-clock support?
stages.excel:
Reference the retained ApprovedTime detail as HoursByEmployeePeriod. Group by EmployeeID and PayrollPeriodID, Sum RegularHours as RegularHours and Sum OvertimeHours as OvertimeHours. Create a separate reference of ApprovedTime named CentersByEmployeePeriod. In this identified-center branch only, filter WorkCenterID to exclude null; keep EmployeeID, PayrollPeriodID, and WorkCenterID, remove duplicate combinations, then group by EmployeeID and PayrollPeriodID and Count Rows as WorkCenters. In another reference of ApprovedTime named UnassignedCenterByEmployeePeriod, retain only null WorkCenterID; group by EmployeeID and PayrollPeriodID, Count Rows as UnassignedTimeEntries, Sum RegularHours as UnassignedRegularHours, and Sum OvertimeHours as UnassignedOvertimeHours. Keep this missing-location evidence separate; do not allocate its hours to identified centers. Left merge CentersByEmployeePeriod into HoursByEmployeePeriod on EmployeeID and PayrollPeriodID and expand WorkCenters. Only in this hours summary, replace a missing WorkCenters count with 0: approved time exists but identifies no center. Import PayrollRegister as PayrollRegisterData and preserve the raw query; reference it as SelectedPayroll and filter periods 1 and 2. Reference SelectedPayroll as PayBridge and Left merge HoursByEmployeePeriod on EmployeeID and PayrollPeriodID, selecting the two keys in that order in both queries. Expand the two hour totals and WorkCenters; load as PayBridge. Keep the 209 register rows and preserve null hours and WorkCenters for registers with no ApprovedTime match; do not invent hours for salaried staff. Load UnassignedCenterByEmployeePeriod separately for review and retain ApprovedTime detail for tracing. Add PayCheck:

~~~text title="Excel — PayBridge[PayCheck]"
=ROUND([@GrossPay]-[@EmployeeWithholdings]-[@NetPay],2)
~~~
stages.check: 209 registers: 104 in period 1 and 105 in period 2. Period 1 gross pay is 125,541.19 and net pay 104,320.59. Period 2 gross pay is 265,084.43 and net pay 220,069.69. Each header’s gross less withholdings equals net.
stages.meaning: The periods differ materially in gross pay. Before calling that an overtime effect, inspect employee populations, hours, pay types, and the first period’s support. Company payroll includes more than Assembly. WorkCenters counts identified centers only. A zero means approved time with no identified center, while a null after the payroll join means no approved hourly support in this scope. Keep both categories separate from identified work centers. Complete the [Lesson 10 summary checkpoint](../../learn-and-practice/follow-hours-into-payroll.md#4-compare-summary-recognition-with-detailed-payment) for a separate period/cost-center population before interpreting ledger payroll. Aggregate the register facts and ledger account independently. A PayrollSummary source ID is not PayrollRegisterID.

stages.mismatch: Do not join payroll headers to raw clock rows. A register repeated ten times would make pay appear ten times too large.

hours groups by EmployeeID and PayrollPeriodID before joining payroll. A null hours result is retained for a register without approved hourly support. COUNT(DISTINCT WorkCenterID) excludes null centers and records identified location variety without repeating pay across locations. It returns zero for an approved-time employee-period with only null centers. The outer payroll join retains null when there is no approved-time employee-period at all. The Excel route retains missing-center evidence in a separate branch.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.

sections.title: Session 3 — Separate settlement and recommend action
sections.intro: Paying employees leaves obligations to tax agencies and benefit providers. Examine both branches, then return to the staffing question.
figure: pay
How do approved hours become pay and cost?
Regular and overtime earnings form gross pay.
Employee deductions reduce gross pay to net pay.
Employer tax and benefits add cost and separate liabilities.

stages.title: Check employee payment completeness
stages.question: Does an approved register prove the employee was paid?
stages.excel: Import PayrollPayment as PayrollPaymentData and preserve the raw query. Reference it as PaymentSchedule and merge to SelectedPayroll on PayrollRegisterID, expand PayrollPeriodID and NetPay, then group by PayrollPeriodID and PaymentDate with count and sum NetPay. Separately reference SelectedPayroll as UnpaidRegisters, Left outer merge to PayrollPaymentData, and filter the expanded PayrollPaymentID to null; retain the unmatched register. stages.keep: Save the payment schedule and one unresolved-payment workpaper.
stages.mismatch: Compare distinct register IDs as well as money. Zero-pay registers can have payment records and should not be silently removed.

LEFT JOIN retains the payroll registers, with a null PayrollPaymentID identifying unmatched payment evidence. This is a test of records in the file, not proof of what happened outside it.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.

stages.title: Reconcile remittances by liability type
stages.question: Why does the tax remittance differ from total employee withholdings?
stages.excel:
Reference the raw PayrollRegisterLineData as LiabilityTotals and merge SelectedPayroll to restrict periods 1 and 2. Filter LineType to Employee Tax Withholding, Benefits Deduction, Employer Payroll Tax, and Employer Benefits. Group by PayrollPeriodID and LineType, summing Amount into a column named Amount; load as LiabilityTotals. Import PayrollLiabilityRemittance as PayrollLiabilityRemittanceData. Reference it as Remittances, filter the two periods, and keep RemittanceDate. On Review enter payroll period 1 in B12. Label B13 Employee tax, B14 Employer tax, and B15 Combined benefits. Enter the following formula in each labeled cell:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B13"
=SUMIFS(LiabilityTotals[Amount],LiabilityTotals[PayrollPeriodID],$B$12,LiabilityTotals[LineType],"Employee Tax Withholding")
~~~



~~~text title="Excel — Review!B14"
=SUMIFS(LiabilityTotals[Amount],LiabilityTotals[PayrollPeriodID],$B$12,LiabilityTotals[LineType],"Employer Payroll Tax")
~~~



~~~text title="Excel — Review!B15"
=SUMIFS(LiabilityTotals[Amount],LiabilityTotals[PayrollPeriodID],$B$12,LiabilityTotals[LineType],"Benefits Deduction")+SUMIFS(LiabilityTotals[Amount],LiabilityTotals[PayrollPeriodID],$B$12,LiabilityTotals[LineType],"Employer Benefits")
~~~

title: Explain Profit, Cash, and the Year-End Close
question: How can the company report profit while cash falls, and what does the year-end close change?
scenario: The controller is preparing the year-end management review. Management wants an explanation of performance, cash movement, and obligations. A collection of reports is not enough: you must reconcile the periods, trace selected source evidence, and decide which unresolved matters deserve attention first. Predict why closing revenue and expense accounts should not itself create or consume cash.
scope: Fourth-quarter 2026 activity and December 31 balances. Opening balances include all recorded history before October 1, including the opening journal and earlier years. The fixed-asset extension follows asset 18 across its 2026 lifecycle. Exclude the working file's later 2027 supplier payments from year-end balances.
deliverable: A full-history balance rollforward, profit/cash bridge, selected source reconciliation, and management review memo.

sections.title: Session 1 — Establish opening, movement, and closing balances
sections.intro: Create Case07.xlsx or Case07.sql. This case begins with the complete ledger, then summarizes before loading results. Keep one definition of the quarter and one sign convention.
figure: statements
How do source events reach the management review?
Operational documents and finance journals produce ledger entries.
The ledger supplies period activity and cumulative account balances.
Statement definitions select and classify those amounts for interpretation.

stages.title: Build openings from the full history
stages.question: What would be missing if you imported only October–December?
stages.excel:
Import T3_GLEntry into Power Query as LedgerHistory and import Account as AccountData. Keep PostingDate, AccountID, Debit, Credit, SourceDocumentType, SourceDocumentID, VoucherNumber, GLEntryID, and Description; the optional asset trace needs Description. Set PostingDate to Date and monetary columns to Decimal Number. Filter only the upper boundary: PostingDate on or before December 31, 2026. Do not add an October lower boundary. In Power Query choose Add Column → Custom Column and add DebitNet using the expression below; Power Query expressions do not start with an equals sign:

~~~text title="Power Query — LedgerHistory / DebitNet"
[Debit]-[Credit]
~~~

Add OpeningDebitNet:

~~~text title="Power Query — LedgerHistory / OpeningDebitNet"
if [PostingDate] < #date(2026,10,1) then [DebitNet] else 0
~~~

Add QuarterDebitNet:

~~~text title="Power Query — LedgerHistory / QuarterDebitNet"
if [PostingDate] >= #date(2026,10,1) then [DebitNet] else 0
~~~

 Reference this query as Rollforward. Group by AccountID, summing OpeningDebitNet, QuarterDebitNet, and DebitNet (name the last ClosingDebitNet). Merge AccountData on AccountID and expand AccountNumber, AccountName, NormalBalance. Sort AccountNumber and load only this summary as Rollforward. Keep LedgerHistory as connection-only on Windows; on Mac retain it in the editor and load the grouped result, without loading raw ledger rows to a sheet.
stages.check: 71 accounts have postings. The source has 732,310 rows before October 1 and 83,085 in the quarter. Cash opens at 9,185,795.46, changes by −743,539.66, and closes at 8,442,255.80.
stages.meaning: A cumulative balance needs prior history. Filtering the source to the quarter would make the opening balance zero and turn the quarter’s movement into a false ending balance.
stages.keep: Save Rollforward, source date boundaries, and row-count evidence.
stages.mismatch: Check the Applied Steps list for an accidental lower-date filter. Numeric source dates must be converted to Date before comparison.
stages.sqlText:
The WHERE clause has only an upper date boundary. CASE separates all earlier history from quarter activity. All amounts use debit minus credit, so opening plus movement equals closing on one consistent sign basis.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelInputs: LedgerHistory ← T3_GLEntry and AccountData ← Account (import here)
excelOutputs: LedgerHistory: full history through December 31, 2026; retained ungrouped in Power Query
Rollforward: one row per account; only summary loaded

In Rollforward add Check:

~~~text title="Excel — Rollforward[Check]"
=ROUND([@OpeningDebitNet]+[@QuarterDebitNet]-[@ClosingDebitNet],2)
~~~

On Review label B2 Opening ledger balance, B3 Quarter ledger movement, and B4 Closing ledger balance. Enter each total and confirm it is within one cent of zero:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B2"
=SUM(Rollforward[OpeningDebitNet])
~~~



~~~text title="Excel — Review!B3"
=SUM(Rollforward[QuarterDebitNet])
~~~



~~~text title="Excel — Review!B4"
=SUM(Rollforward[ClosingDebitNet])
~~~

Keep the debit-net columns unchanged. For a management display add NormalClosing:

~~~text title="Excel — Rollforward[NormalClosing]"
=IF([@NormalBalance]="Credit",-[@ClosingDebitNet],[@ClosingDebitNet])
~~~

Filter to account numbers 1020, 2010, 2020, 2040, and 2060 to inspect the control accounts.
stages.check: Closing debit-net values include AR 4,798,804.32; AP −6,237,466.66; GRNI −1,020,992.06; accrued expenses −480,552.36; customer deposits −3,413.46. All 71 opening-plus-movement checks are zero to cents.
stages.meaning: A negative debit-net AP balance is the expected credit balance. Changing signs selectively inside the underlying rollforward would destroy the accounting identity.
stages.keep: Retain the sign definition and selected control-account display.
stages.mismatch: Do not compare a credit-normal report balance to the raw debit-net schedule without reversing its sign.
stages.sqlText: Use the 71 rows returned by c07-rollforward.sql. For each row, OpeningDebitNet plus QuarterDebitNet must equal ClosingDebitNet to cents. Read accounts 1020, 2010, 2020, 2040, and 2060 and reverse the sign only when presenting a credit-normal liability to management. Keep the original debit-net schedule as the reconciliation basis.

sections.stop: Save the 71-account schedule and its checks. You now have a reliable period boundary for the remaining sessions.

sections.title: Session 2 — Explain profit and cash differences
sections.intro: Calculate profit before closing entries, then reconcile it to the cash movement through changes in other accounts. This arithmetic bridge is broader than an operating-cash subtotal.
figure: rollforward
Which history belongs in each column?
Opening: all postings before October 1, 2026.
Movement: October 1–December 31, with close treatment stated.
Closing: opening plus movement through December 31.

stages.title: Calculate pre-close performance and cash activity
stages.question: Would including the annual closing entry make December’s operating result meaningful?
stages.excel:
Import JournalEntry as JournalEntryData and retain its full history. Reference LedgerHistory as LedgerPrepared; merge AccountData and expand AccountNumber, AccountName, AccountType, and AccountSubType. Keep this full-history detail ungrouped. In Power Query add JournalKey with Add Column → Custom Column:

~~~text title="Power Query — ProfitDetail / JournalKey"
if [SourceDocumentType] = "JournalEntry" then [SourceDocumentID] else null
~~~

 Left merge JournalEntryData on JournalKey = JournalEntryID and expand EntryType; do not merge every source ID to journals. Reference LedgerPrepared as QuarterLedger; filter PostingDate October 1–December 31, 2026, and exclude EntryType beginning Year-End Close while keeping null EntryType. Preserve QuarterLedger ungrouped, with all account types. Reference QuarterLedger as ProfitDetail and filter AccountType Revenue or Expense and AccountSubType not Header. Add a Custom Column named ProfitAmount:

~~~text title="Power Query — ProfitDetail / ProfitAmount"
[Credit]-[Debit]
~~~

Reference ProfitDetail as ProfitSummary. Derive Month using Transform → Date → Month → Start of Month and group by Month summing ProfitAmount into a column named ProfitAmount. Load the three-row summary as ProfitSummary. For CashActivity, reference QuarterLedger, filter AccountNumber 1010, group by SourceDocumentType summing Debit, Credit, and DebitNet into columns with those same names. Load as CashActivity.
stages.check: Pre-close profit: October 255,812.14; November 405,751.40; December 502,693.70; quarter 1,164,257.24. Cash falls 743,539.66. Customer cash receipts add 7,816,054.56; supplier payments use 5,912,239.65.
stages.meaning: Profit and cash are different measures of the same business period. Customer receipts and supplier payments may settle invoices or obligations from earlier periods. The annual close must not erase the quarter’s performance measure.
stages.keep: Save monthly Profit and CashActivity with the close exclusion documented.
stages.mismatch: Preserve null journal matches for operational events. Filtering null EntryType out would remove much of the ledger.
stages.sqlText:
The journal join applies only when the source type is JournalEntry. COALESCE preserves operational entries with no journal match, while NOT LIKE excludes the annual close. Profit uses credit minus debit for revenue and expense accounts.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelInputs: JournalEntryData ← JournalEntry (import here; full history retained)
excelOutputs: LedgerPrepared: full-history detail with account and conditional journal fields
QuarterLedger: all account types in Q4, excluding close; retained ungrouped
CashActivity: Q4 cash by source type

stages.title: Construct the complete arithmetic bridge
stages.question: Which other account changes explain the difference?
stages.excel:
Reference the retained QuarterLedger as BridgeEffects; it already has the conditional journal join and close exclusion, with all account types still present. Keep AccountNumber not 1010 and AccountType other than Revenue or Expense. In Power Query add BridgeEffect with Add Column → Custom Column:

~~~text title="Power Query — Bridge effects / BridgeEffect"
[Credit]-[Debit]
~~~

Group by AccountNumber and AccountName, summing BridgeEffect into a column with the same name. Add NonzeroEffect with the expression below and filter it to true:

~~~text title="Power Query — Bridge effects / NonzeroEffect"
Number.Round(Number.Abs([BridgeEffect]),2) > 0
~~~

Load as BridgeEffects. On Review label B8 Quarter pre-close profit and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B8"
=SUM(ProfitSummary[ProfitAmount])
~~~

Place the 19 effect rows beneath the profit explanation. Label B9 Calculated cash movement and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B9"
=SUM(B8,BridgeEffects[BridgeEffect])
~~~

Label B10 Ledger cash movement and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B10"
=SUM(CashActivity[DebitNet])
~~~

Label B11 Bridge difference and enter:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B11"
=ROUND(B9-B10,2)
~~~

Chart the signed effects using a column chart, clearly separating starting profit and calculated cash movement from individual effects.
stages.check: Nineteen nonzero account effects sum to −1,907,796.90. Added to profit of 1,164,257.24, they reconcile to −743,539.66 cash movement. Inventory and WIP increases contribute −2,872,614.48; the AP increase contributes +411,484.70.
stages.meaning: This bridge explains the accounting difference. It does not mean every inventory increase was paid in cash or every liability increase is an operating cash inflow. The published cash-flow statement applies its own operating, investing, and financing classifications.
stages.keep: Save the zero-difference bridge and identify the largest three effects.
stages.mismatch: Do not use post-close retained-earnings movement as an additional profit effect: that would count annual profit again.
stages.sqlText:
Exclude cash and revenue/expense accounts, keep quarter activity, and remove annual close entries. Credit minus debit on the remaining accounts supplies the effects needed to bridge pre-close profit to cash. HAVING removes immaterial zero aggregates after grouping.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.

stages.title: Trace one liability movement to source documents
stages.question: Can the large GRNI entries be explained by a receipt and a later invoice?

Reference LedgerPrepared as LiabilityTrace and filter AccountNumber 2020 and December 1–31, 2026. In Power Query add a Custom Column named AbsoluteAmount:

~~~text title="Power Query — Selected liability trace / AbsoluteAmount"
Number.Abs([DebitNet])

Reference PurchaseInvoiceLineData as ReceiptInvoiceTrace, filter PurchaseInvoiceID 39692, merge GoodsReceiptLineData on GoodsReceiptLineID, then GoodsReceiptData on GoodsReceiptID.

The supplier invoice header is dated December 30 while its GRNI ledger posting is December 31; retain both dates rather than silently substituting one.

stages.keep: Save the two-document trace and identify the next table needed to investigate payment.
stages.mismatch: Matching amounts alone are insufficient. Require the GoodsReceiptLineID relationship.

sections.title: Session 3 — Separate annual close from quarterly performance
sections.intro: The close transfers a year’s profit into equity. Its scope is the entire year, even though its posting date falls in the fourth quarter.
figure: close
What does the annual closing sequence do?
Journal 850 closes annual revenue and expense balances into income summary.
Journal 851 transfers 4,503,611.24 from income summary to retained earnings.
Quarterly performance remains the pre-close activity, not the transfer to equity.

stages.title: Inspect both closing journals
stages.question: Should the equity transfer equal fourth-quarter profit or full-year profit?
stages.excel:
Reference the raw JournalEntryData as ClosingJournals and filter PostingDate December 31, 2026 and EntryType beginning Year-End Close. Reference LedgerPrepared as ClosingJournalDetail, filter SourceDocumentType JournalEntry, and Inner merge ClosingJournals on SourceDocumentID = JournalEntryID. Keep all account lines; AccountNumber and DebitNet are already present from LedgerPrepared. Expand JournalEntryID from ClosingJournals and keep the existing EntryType; retain SourceDocumentType and SourceDocumentID as the source pair.

Reference ClosingJournalDetail as ClosingJournalSummary and group by JournalEntryID, EntryType, AccountNumber, summing DebitNet. Separately reference LedgerPrepared as FullYearPerformance and filter PostingDate January 1–December 31, 2026, without a quarter restriction. Add ProfitAmount using the expression below:

~~~text title="Power Query — Full-year performance / ProfitAmount"
[Credit]-[Debit]
~~~

 Filter AccountType Revenue or Expense and AccountSubType not Header. Add a custom column ReviewYear with the constant 2026. Preserve FullYearPerformance and create two references: AnnualPreClose excludes EntryType beginning Year-End Close while keeping null EntryType; AnnualPostClose keeps closing entries. In each reference Group By ReviewYear and sum ProfitAmount as AnnualProfit. Keep both one-row results for comparison.

stages.meaning: A zero post-close P&L balance confirms the transfer for the selected definition without implying that the business earned no profit. Do not add the annual transfer to the quarter’s operating result.
stages.keep: Save the closing sequence and annual comparison.
stages.mismatch: An annual close cannot be checked against a quarter-only P&L. Keep annual and quarterly schedules distinctly labeled.
stages.sqlText: Run each statement separately in the SQL editor. Save its text and result with the stage title. Read the result at the grain described in the question and compare the checkpoint before continuing.

sections.title: Session 4 — Reconcile reports and advise management

How should management read the quarter?
Pre-close profit is 1,164,257.24.
Other account effects explain why cash movement is −743,539.66.
Cash closes at 8,442,255.80; outstanding obligations require separate follow-up.

title: Investigate Exceptions and Recommend Controls
question: Which query flags become supported findings, and what control could be assessed?
scenario: The controller requests a focused controls review. Investigate alternative explanations for each flag before deciding what the evidence establishes. You will examine repeated supplier references and overtime approval support, then recommend controls with a clear owner, procedure, and assessment method.
scope: Duplicate supplier invoice and check references across the entire recorded history, plus approved overtime entries with positive overtime dated October 1–December 31, 2026. These populations have different denominators. The review uses source records, not instructor anomaly labels or the support workbook.
deliverable: An exception register, two source-supported workpapers, and prioritized control recommendations.

sections.title: Session 1 — Define risks, criteria, and evidence
sections.intro: Create Case08.xlsx or Case08.sql and a Review note. Use four conclusion categories: supported exception, explained timing or valid circumstance, unresolved evidence, and no exception under the stated test. A query flag is the starting point.
figure: risk
What turns a risk into an investigation?
Define the risk and the criterion to test.
Select a population with a stated denominator and date boundary.
Collect source evidence before classifying a finding.

stages.title: Specify two review criteria
stages.question: Could the same number of flags mean different things in different populations?
stages.excel:
Import PurchaseInvoice as PurchaseInvoiceData without a date filter. Import DisbursementPayment as DisbursementPaymentData without removing rows; retain both complete raw queries. Create a Reference named CheckPayments, filter CheckNumber not blank, and load that reference for the check-reference test. Keep the original query available for invoice payment investigations. Import TimeClockEntry as TimeClockEntryData; preserve the raw query and reference it as Overtime, filtered WorkDate October 1–December 31, 2026, ClockStatus Approved, and OvertimeHours greater than zero. Load the last selection as Overtime. On Review label B2 Invoice documents, B3 Payments with a check reference, and B4 Approved overtime records. Enter the counts:

~~~text title="Excel — Review!B2"
=ROWS(PurchaseInvoiceData[PurchaseInvoiceID])
~~~



~~~text title="Excel — Review!B3"
=ROWS(CheckPayments[DisbursementID])
~~~



~~~text title="Excel — Review!B4"
=ROWS(Overtime[TimeClockEntryID])
~~~

 For the invoice test define a repeated reference as the same SupplierID and exact InvoiceNumber occurring more than once; for checks use SupplierID and nonblank CheckNumber. For overtime, first test missing linked approval or hours above linked ApprovedHours. Treat identity, status, and timing as further evidence checks.

stages.meaning: The tests do not cover every AP or payroll risk. Note that exact reference matching misses differently formatted duplicates before interpreting a zero or low rate.
