sections.title: Session 2 — Investigate repeated AP references
sections.intro: A repeated reference may indicate a duplicate document, a reused reference, or a recording problem. Inspect the linked commercial evidence and payments before alleging duplicate payment.
figure: ap
What evidence distinguishes a repeated reference from duplicate payment?
Group invoice or check references within the same supplier.
Read each flagged document, its receipt links, and payment trail.
Classify what repeats and what additional evidence is required.

stages.title: Find groups without multiplying documents
stages.question: Should the denominator count duplicate groups or document rows?
stages.excel: In Power Query Reference PurchaseInvoiceData as InvoiceGroups. Group by SupplierID and InvoiceNumber; Count Rows as Occurrences; filter Occurrences greater than 1. Reference InvoiceGroups as DuplicateInvoices and Inner merge to PurchaseInvoiceData on both keys; expand the document columns. Separately reference CheckPayments as CheckGroups, group by SupplierID and CheckNumber, Count Rows as Occurrences, and retain counts greater than 1. Reference CheckGroups as DuplicateChecks and Inner merge to CheckPayments on both keys; expand the document columns. Reference DisbursementPaymentData as PaymentsByInvoice, group by PurchaseInvoiceID and Sum Amount as PaidAmount, then Left merge that unique-key summary to DuplicateInvoices. Keep the grouped-key queries and full source queries available; load DuplicateInvoices and DuplicateChecks for inspection.
stages.check: Six invoice-reference groups contain 12 invoice rows. Two check-reference groups contain four payment rows. The first invoice pair is supplier 1, reference V0001-2024-000028, invoice IDs 28 and 44.
stages.meaning: Twelve flagged invoice rows and six groups are different counts. A percentage based on groups divided by document rows would mix units. Keep the invoice and payment flag rates separate.
stages.keep: Save both group lists and all flagged document rows.
stages.mismatch: Group within supplier. A reference repeated by two different suppliers is not the same test. Exclude blank check references explicitly.
stages.sqlText:
groups identifies exact supplier/reference pairs occurring more than once. Joining the group back retrieves each flagged document. The payment SUM is independent, so multiple payments cannot duplicate invoice values.

Blank references are excluded before grouping. The same supplier and CheckNumber must match. Retain both group counts and payment-row counts because they answer different questions.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelOutputs: InvoiceGroups and CheckGroups: repeated document references
DuplicateInvoices and DuplicateChecks: document-level exception evidence

stages.title: Follow the first invoice pair to receipts and payment
stages.question: Do invoices 28 and 44 represent the same goods and amount?
stages.excel: Import PurchaseInvoiceLine as PurchaseInvoiceLineData; reference it as InvoicePairLines and filter PurchaseInvoiceID 28 or 44. Keep GoodsReceiptLineID, POLineID, ItemID, Quantity, and LineTotal. Reference the original DisbursementPaymentData as InvoicePairPayments and filter to those same invoice IDs without the nonblank-check filter; these payments may use another method. Compare document dates and amounts, receipt links, and payment IDs. Retain a separate register row for each invoice.
stages.check: Invoice 28 is 629.94 for item 220, receipt line 48; invoice 44 is 1,504.07 for item 193, receipt line 41. Payments 127 and 51 settle the different amounts on April 1 and March 23.
stages.meaning: The repeated invoice reference is supported. The different amounts, items, and receipt links weaken the claim that these are duplicate economic transactions. The source data alone does not show the supplier’s original invoice images or a bank confirmation.
stages.keep: Write Workpaper A: criterion, flagged keys, source trail, alternative explanation, conclusion, missing evidence, and next action.
stages.mismatch: A paid status or matching reference cannot establish duplicate payment. Do not sum the pair and label it a proven loss.

stages.title: Investigate the repeated check example
stages.question: Does one repeated check reference establish that the bank paid twice?
stages.excel:
In DuplicateChecks filter SupplierID 1 and CheckNumber CHK0006076. Inspect DisbursementIDs 6076 and 6107, their PurchaseInvoiceIDs, PaymentDate, Amount, and ClearedDate. Add InvoiceNumber to DuplicateChecks:

~~~text title="Excel — DuplicateChecks[InvoiceNumber]"
=XLOOKUP([@PurchaseInvoiceID],PurchaseInvoiceData[PurchaseInvoiceID],PurchaseInvoiceData[InvoiceNumber],"No match",0)
~~~

Add InvoiceGrandTotal:

~~~text title="Excel — DuplicateChecks[InvoiceGrandTotal]"
=XLOOKUP([@PurchaseInvoiceID],PurchaseInvoiceData[PurchaseInvoiceID],PurchaseInvoiceData[GrandTotal],"No match",0)
~~~

 Compare with the invoice-reference workpaper, keeping the two criteria separate.
stages.check: The two payment rows refer to invoices 3101 and 4070, amounts 1,468.04 and 1,104.48, both dated January 1, 2025, with different cleared dates.
stages.meaning: The repeated check reference warrants treasury/AP follow-up. Distinct payment rows and clearing fields still do not replace external banking evidence. Classify the reference exception as supported and the duplicate-cash-loss claim as unresolved.
stages.keep: Retain the payment pair and specify the bank or supplier evidence needed.
stages.mismatch: Do not confuse CheckNumber with the unique DisbursementID.
stages.sqlText: Return to c08-checks.sql. Read the two rows with CheckNumber CHK0006076 and compare their invoice IDs, dates, amounts, and cleared dates. Keep this check-reference investigation separate from the invoice-reference workpaper.

sections.stop: Save Workpaper A and both AP exception registers. Your conclusion must separate a confirmed reference problem from an unproven loss.

sections.title: Session 3 — Investigate overtime approval support
sections.intro: Approved payroll time and a linked overtime approval are different records. A positive overtime amount can be approved for pay while its separate authorization link is missing.
figure: overtime
Which approval supports the overtime hours?
Select approved time entries with positive overtime in the defined quarter.
Left join the linked overtime approval so missing links remain visible.
Inspect hours, identity, period, dates, and status before concluding.

stages.title: Classify the hours test
stages.question: Why would an Inner join hide the very exception you want to inspect?
stages.excel:
Import OvertimeApproval as Approvals. In Power Query Left outer merge Overtime to Approvals on OvertimeApprovalID. Expand the approval ID as MatchedApprovalID, ApprovedHours, ApprovedDate as OvertimeApprovedDate, and Status. Keep the time record’s original ApprovedDate separately. Load as OvertimeReview. Add HoursTest:

~~~text title="Excel — OvertimeReview[HoursTest]"
=IF([@MatchedApprovalID]="","Missing linked approval",IF([@ApprovedHours]<[@OvertimeHours],"Hours exceed approval","Hours supported"))
~~~

Create a PivotTable with HoursTest in Rows and Count of TimeClockEntryID in Values. Preserve zero approved hours as a real value.
stages.check: 1,895 eligible time entries: 336 missing linked approval, zero with hours exceeding a linked approval, and 1,559 with hours supported. The missing-link rate is 17.73% of eligible entries.
stages.meaning: These 336 time entries lack a linked approval record under this test; this does not establish that the associated employees lacked authorization outside the file. The 1,559 hours-supported rows still need identity, status, and date checks for a fuller authorization conclusion.
stages.keep: Save the complete classification and the flagged subset with stable IDs.
stages.mismatch: Keep null matches. A zero-row exception list after an Inner join is not evidence of effective control.
stages.sqlText:
LEFT JOIN retains missing approvals. CASE applies the hours-support criteria in order: no linked record, insufficient approved hours, then hours supported. The WHERE clause fixes the eligible quarter, approved clock status, and positive overtime denominator.

Run each complete statement separately and retain its result before continuing.
excelOutputs: OvertimeReview: time-entry detail and approval match; HoursTest classification

stages.title: Compare a flag with an hours-supported record
stages.question: What does the comparison reveal about the limits of the first test?
stages.excel: Filter OvertimeReview to TimeClockEntryIDs 49436 and 49581. Return to the merge expansion and add EmployeeID as ApprovalEmployeeID, PayrollPeriodID as ApprovalPeriodID, and WorkDate as ApprovalWorkDate from Approvals, keeping time-record values beside them. Compare employee, period, work date, status, and approval date. For the flagged record, retain blank approval fields and request supporting evidence rather than filling them from a nearby employee or day.
stages.check: Entry 49436 is employee 17’s 4.50 overtime hours on October 1, linked to approval 16587 for 4.50 hours. Entry 49581 is employee 18’s 0.34 overtime hours on October 5 with no linked overtime approval.
stages.meaning: The comparison supports a missing-link finding for 49581 under this review’s criterion. It does not prove the work was not performed, the employee was overpaid, or anyone acted dishonestly.
stages.keep: Write Workpaper B with the tested criterion, both records, the evidence gap, and a proposed follow-up.
stages.mismatch: Do not use an anomaly label as evidence. Compare source fields and distinguish a missing record from a contradictory record.

sections.title: Session 4 — Prioritize findings and design assessable controls
sections.intro: The final task is a reasoned recommendation. Count and amount can help prioritize follow-up, but frequency alone is not a measure of proven financial loss.
figure: finding
How should an exception be classified?
Flag: the query criterion identifies a record.
Investigation: compare supporting documents and alternative explanations.
Conclusion: supported exception, explained circumstance, unresolved evidence, or no exception under the test.

stages.title: Build a prioritized exception register
stages.question: Which issue warrants immediate evidence collection, and which warrants a process improvement?
stages.excel: Create an ExceptionRegister table with FindingID, Test, Population, SourceKeys, ObservedCondition, Evidence, AlternativeExplanation, ConclusionCategory, PotentialConsequence, Owner, and NextAction. Enter the worked AP pair, repeated-check pair, and overtime comparison. Keep potential consequences as hypotheses unless amounts are supported. Rank follow-ups using urgency, plausible impact, and ease of obtaining decisive evidence; explain the ranking in prose rather than inventing a numeric risk score.
stages.check: The worked evidence supports repeated references and missing approval links. It leaves duplicate economic loss and off-system authorization unresolved.
stages.meaning: A reasonable priority is to obtain supplier/bank evidence for repeated payment references and restore verifiable overtime authorization links before claiming loss or misconduct. Other priorities are acceptable if they explain impact and uncertainty.
stages.keep: Save the exception register and a brief prioritization rationale.
stages.mismatch: Do not combine the 336 overtime flags and 16 AP document flags into one overall exception rate.
stages.sqlText: Use the saved result tables from the preceding stages to construct this comparison and written interpretation. Retain the query names, filters, source keys, and amounts in your case notes. An ordered result table can communicate the comparison without making a chart or switching tools.
excelInputs: Earlier AP/check/overtime workpapers with their separate populations
excelOutputs: ExceptionRegister: bounded findings and follow-up priorities

stages.title: Propose controls that can be tested
stages.question: What would a reviewer observe to determine whether your proposed control operated?
stages.excel: Create a ControlReview table with Risk, ProposedControl, Owner, Frequency, RetainedEvidence, PopulationForTesting, TestProcedure, and FailureCriterion. For AP, propose checking supplier/reference uniqueness before posting, with documented review of legitimate repeated references. For overtime, propose checking employee, period, date, approved hours, and approval status before payroll release, with an explicit late-approval escalation. State these as proposed controls; the case has not established an existing company policy. Include a retrospective sample test and a repeatable population query as complementary procedures.
stages.check: An assessable recommendation identifies who performs the check, when it occurs, what evidence is retained, and what constitutes failure. A lower flag count alone is not sufficient: deleted or disconnected records could also reduce it.
stages.meaning: For AP, inspect recorded review/override evidence for a sample of repeated references and verify all invoices remain in the population. For overtime, trace selected paid hours to valid approvals and inspect escalation evidence. Test both flagged and unflagged records.
stages.keep: Write a 600–800 word controls memo with two workpapers, priorities, proposed controls, and test procedures.
stages.mismatch: A recommendation to “improve controls” is incomplete without an owner, evidence, and a criterion a reviewer can assess.
stages.sqlText: Use the saved result tables from the preceding stages to construct this comparison and written interpretation. Retain the query names, filters, source keys, and amounts in your case notes. An ordered result table can communicate the comparison without making a chart or switching tools.
excelOutputs: ControlReview: proposed controls, test populations, procedures, and failure criteria

sections.stop: Save both workpapers, the register, and controls memo. Your independent challenge begins with new evidence and no public model conclusion.

interpretation: The worked review demonstrates why a flag is not a finding about fraud or financial loss. Repeated references and missing approval links are supported conditions whose economic consequences require additional evidence. Controls become useful recommendations when the owner, timing, evidence, test population, and failure criteria are explicit.
challenge: Investigate Q3 2026 overtime using the same eligibility and hours-support criteria. For AP, define a new review of supplier invoice references within 2025 and investigate any flagged groups, or document a clean result. Keep denominators distinct and justify your follow-up priorities.
hint: A new population can produce fewer flags, different explanations, or no exceptions. Evaluate evidence completeness before treating a zero result as assurance. Preserve all eligible records when joining support.
